title: Instruction-Aware Cooperative TLB and Cache Replacement Policies
problem: Modern server and data center applications have large instruction footprints that cause frequent instruction-side TLB and cache misses, with instruction TLB (iTLB) misses being particularly harmful because they cause pipeline stalls that block forward progress. Existing TLB and cache replacement policies treat instruction and data streams equivalently and do not account for the criticality of instruction accesses.
method: The paper proposes instruction-aware cooperative replacement policies that distinguish instruction accesses from data accesses in both the TLB and cache. The cooperative approach coordinates eviction decisions between the iTLB and the instruction cache (iCache), so that evicting a page from the iTLB also triggers or informs iCache eviction decisions and vice versa, reducing redundant refills. Replacement decisions are guided by instruction-access frequency and recency, with policy cooperation preventing the two structures from working at cross-purposes during instruction working set thrashing.

title: Cascade: A Dependency-aware Efficient Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Network
problem: TGNN training is severely constrained by temporal dependencies between input events: large batches improve parallelism but cause infrequent node memory updates leading to stale information and accuracy degradation, forcing small-batch training with high latency and underutilized hardware.
method: Cascade uses a topology-aware scheduler that packs as many spatially-independent events as possible into the same batch, then leverages inter-node memory similarity to identify 'stabilized' nodes whose memories have converged sufficiently to safely break temporal dependencies. This similarity-based dependency breaking allows temporally-independent events to be included in larger batches. An adaptive update frequency mechanism based on runtime feedback further reduces redundant memory updates, achieving 2.3x average (up to 5.1x) speedup without accuracy loss.

title: Dilu: Enabling GPU Resourcing-on-Demand for Serverless DL Serving via Introspective Elasticity
problem: Serverless DL serving systems use coarse-grained static GPU allocation that produces 15-94% GPU fragmentation due to dynamic workload patterns; existing horizontal-only scaling cannot adapt GPU resource allocation fine-grainedly within a running DL function instance, degrading utilization and violating QoS.
method: Dilu introduces Introspective Elasticity (IE), a two-dimensional co-scaling mechanism combining vertical scaling (adjusting GPU resource allocation within a running DL task) and horizontal scaling (adding/removing instances). Dilu uses multi-factor profiling with efficient pruning search to characterize each DL function's GPU compute/memory sensitivity. A cross-layer scheduler applies resourcing-complementary principles to fill fragmented GPU capacity with compatible DL tasks. At runtime, an adaptive 2D co-scaling controller continuously monitors QoS signals and adjusts both per-instance GPU allocation and the number of instances to minimize fragmentation while meeting SLAs.

title: Efficient Memory Side-Channel Protection for Embedding Generation in Machine Learning
problem: Embedding table lookups in ML models (DLRMs, LLMs) leak sensitive input features (user IDs, token indices) through memory access patterns, making them vulnerable to side-channel attacks; protecting these accesses with conventional ORAM incurs prohibitive overhead due to the massive size of embedding tables.
method: The paper evaluates three protection strategies: (1) linear scan of the embedding table (accesses all rows, hiding which row is used); (2) ORAM protection with optimized implementation; and (3) Deep Hash Embedding (DHE), which replaces the table lookup entirely with a hash-based neural network computation that takes the embedding index as input and produces an embedding vector through compute rather than memory access, eliminating the memory access pattern. A hybrid scheme combines DHE for large embedding tables (where its compute cost is amortized) with linear scan for small tables, selected per table based on profiled break-even points.

title: ColumnDisturb: Understanding Column-based Read Disturbance in Real DRAM Chips and Implications for Future Systems
problem: A newly discovered DRAM read disturbance phenomenon called ColumnDisturb allows a single aggressor row activation to disturb DRAM cells through bitlines (columns), inducing bitflips in rows sharing the same columns across multiple subarrays — up to 3072 rows simultaneously in DDR4 — which is fundamentally different from RowHammer/RowPress that affect only a few adjacent rows in a single subarray.
method: The paper conducts a rigorous experimental characterization of ColumnDisturb on 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major DRAM manufacturers. Experiments vary temperature, data patterns, DRAM timing parameters (tRCD, tRAS, tRP), average bitline voltage, memory access patterns, and spatial variation across chips. The study measures minimum time to first bitflip, affected row count, and bitflip counts under nominal 63.6ms DDR4 refresh windows. The authors compare ColumnDisturb severity against DRAM retention failures and perform cycle-level simulation to quantify the impact on retention-aware refresh mechanisms that propose to skip refreshes for cells with long retention times.

title: ATiM: Autotuning Tensor Programs for Processing-in-DRAM
problem: Current software stacks for DRAM-PIM (specifically UPMEM) rely on hand-tuned libraries, lack high-level programming abstractions, and have no systematic optimization framework, making it difficult to achieve peak hardware utilization for tensor workloads including LLM layers.
method: ATiM is a search-based optimizing tensor compiler for the UPMEM DRAM-PIM architecture. It jointly searches the host-side and kernel-side tensor program space, applying PIM-aware optimizations to handle boundary conditions introduced by the banked DRAM layout. The compiler extends standard autotuning search algorithms to cover the expanded UPMEM-specific search space (e.g., tasklet counts, loop tiling, data placement across DPU banks), then generates fused, hardware-specific code without requiring manual library authoring.

title: CORDOBA: Carbon-Efficient Optimization Framework for Computing Systems
problem: Optimizing the carbon footprint of computing systems across large hardware design spaces is intractable with existing methods because it requires simultaneously trading off operational carbon, embodied carbon, performance, power, and area (PPA) under uncertainty in carbon intensity parameters.
method: CORDOBA introduces the total Carbon Delay Product (tCDP) metric — product of total lifecycle carbon (operational + embodied) and application execution time — as a single scalar objective for carbon-efficient hardware optimization. The framework performs design-space exploration by sweeping hardware configurations (e.g., core count, memory hierarchy, 2D vs. 3D integration via chiplet stacking) and evaluating tCDP under parametric uncertainty in carbon intensity, eliminating up to 98% of the design space as Pareto-dominated. Two case studies apply CORDOBA to real CPU systems: halving cores from 8 to 4 and adopting 3D-stacked logic+memory integration.

title: Neuralink: Fast on-Device LLM Inference with Neuron Co-Activation Linking
problem: On-device LLM inference on smartphones using sparsity-based techniques (loading only active neurons from flash) suffers from excessive random I/O operations due to scattered neuron placement in flash, and smartphones face severe IOPS constraints that make these I/O patterns a critical bottleneck.
method: Neuralink reorganizes neuron placement in flash storage offline based on neuron co-activation patterns: neurons that are frequently activated together are linked contiguously in flash, enabling sequential read access that is orders of magnitude more efficient than random IOPS on mobile flash. An online stage then uses tailored data access and caching strategies aligned with the sequential layout and hardware characteristics of the target phone. The two-stage pipeline (offline co-activation profiling and layout reorganization; online cache-friendly sequential access) reduces I/O operations for sparsity-based LLM inference.

title: ARC: Warp-level Adaptive Atomic Reduction in GPUs to Accelerate Differentiable Rendering
problem: During the backward pass of rasterization-based differentiable rendering (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting), gradient computation requires a large volume of atomic add operations to accumulate gradients from many Gaussian primitives into shared parameters, overwhelming the atomic units in the GPU L2 cache and causing long stalls that dominate training time.
method: ARC introduces warp-level adaptive atomic reduction, a GPU microarchitecture extension that intercepts atomic add operations at the warp level before they reach the L2 cache atomic units. Within a warp, threads targeting the same memory address are first reduced together using warp-level shuffle instructions (or a small dedicated reduction buffer), producing a single atomic operation per warp instead of one per thread. The approach adaptively decides whether to apply warp-level reduction based on detected contention levels, avoiding overhead when atomics are already sparse.

title: UniZK: Accelerating Zero-Knowledge Proof with Unified Hardware and Flexible Kernel Mapping
problem: Emerging hash-function-based ZKP protocols introduce diverse computation kernels (NTT, hash functions, general polynomial arithmetic) that existing ZKP accelerators cannot efficiently support, since prior designs target only elliptic-curve-based protocols with dedicated per-kernel hardware units that waste area and underutilize resources for multi-kernel workloads.
method: UniZK uses a systolic-array-based hardware architecture enhanced with extra local links and a new vector processing mode that makes the array flexible enough to serve as a unified substrate for diverse ZKP kernels. Novel mapping strategies are developed to map NTT, hash functions, and general polynomial computations onto this unified hardware, ensuring high resource utilization without dedicated per-kernel units. Smart kernel mapping strategies handle the varied data flow and compute patterns of each primitive.

title: UGPU: Dynamically Constructing Unbalanced GPUs for Enhanced Resource Efficiency
problem: Physical GPUs maintain a fixed, balanced ratio of compute and memory resources, which is inefficient when co-executing workloads have heterogeneous compute-to-memory demands. Partitioning a GPU into unbalanced slices requires accurate performance prediction under variable resource allocations and causes heavy data migration overhead when memory resources are redistributed.
method: UGPU dynamically carves a single physical GPU into unbalanced GPU slices—each with a tailored compute-SM count and HBM capacity—using a demand-aware resource partitioning algorithm that avoids complex analytical performance models. To handle memory redistribution without incurring the latency of traditional page migration, it introduces PageMove, which exploits the fact that all HBM memory channels share physical TSV connections within the DRAM stack, enabling parallel page migration between bank groups. PageMove pairs a customized memory address mapping with a Parallel Page Migration Mode (PPMM) and updated virtual memory management to move pages across memory dies at high throughput concurrently.

title: Neo: Towards Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration using Tensor Core
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes massive computational overhead—orders of magnitude over plaintext computation—that prevents practical deployment, while existing ASIC accelerators lack generality as FHE algorithms rapidly evolve. GPU-based solutions exist but fail to exploit tensor core (TCU) hardware for the dominant FHE primitives.
method: Neo maps the CKKS FHE scheme's core operations—Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and polynomial multiplication—onto GPU Tensor Cores (TCUs) by reformulating them as matrix operations compatible with the TCU's INT8/FP16 matrix-multiply-accumulate pipeline. The design includes careful decomposition of NTT butterfly stages and residue number system (RNS) arithmetic to fit TCU matrix dimensions, with custom CUDA kernels orchestrating data layout, twiddle factor injection, and modular reduction to avoid overflow in low-precision arithmetic.

title: TAPAS: Thermal- and Power-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference in Cloud Platforms
problem: LLM inference workloads exhibit fine-grained millisecond-scale phase transitions (prefill vs. decode) with distinct thermal and power profiles, which traditional cloud thermal and power management techniques are too coarse-grained to handle effectively. Cloud co-location of SaaS and IaaS workloads with differing visibility levels further complicates scheduling.
method: TAPAS is a thermal- and power-aware scheduler for LLM inference that models the per-phase (prefill/decode) thermal and power profiles of inference workloads at millisecond granularity. It leverages LLM configuration parameters (model parallelism, model size, quantization level) as scheduling knobs to trade off performance, temperature, power consumption, and output quality. The scheduler accounts for co-located SaaS and IaaS workloads, applying different control strategies depending on the level of visibility and flexibility available for each workload type.

title: Rethinking Prefetching for Intermittent Computing
problem: Conventional hardware prefetchers are energy-wasteful on batteryless energy harvesting systems (EHSs) because they aggressively fetch cache lines that are lost on power failure before any hit, wasting harvested energy. Frequent outages on EHSs mean that prefetched data that is never accessed before the next power loss represents pure energy overhead.
method: IPEX (Intermittence-aware Prefetching EXtension) is an add-on layer that wraps existing prefetchers on EHSs without replacing them. It tracks which prefetched cache blocks receive a hit before a power failure and suppresses future prefetches of lines that historically go unused ('useless prefetches'). Additionally, IPEX monitors harvested energy levels to predict imminent outages and dynamically throttles the prefetch degree at that moment, targeting only blocks likely to be accessed before power loss. The result is that harvested energy is redirected from futile prefetches toward productive forward execution progress.

title: Orion: A Fully Homomorphic Encryption Framework for Deep Learning
problem: Mapping arbitrary deep neural networks to Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) primitives is intractable with existing tools because FHE requires packing large vectors, managing noise budget through bootstrap placement, and translating general convolutions to the limited FHE instruction set—challenges that have limited FHE neural inference to shallow or small networks.
method: Orion is an automated compiler that accepts PyTorch DNNs and emits FHE programs. It introduces a single-shot multiplexed packing strategy for arbitrary convolution layers that avoids the combinatorial explosion of prior slot-packing schemes. Orion also introduces an automated bootstrap placement algorithm with scale management that tracks noise accumulation across layers and inserts bootstrapping operations at minimum-cost positions. Together these enable end-to-end compilation of deep networks (ResNet-20, ResNet-50, YOLO-v1 with 139M parameters) without manual FHE engineering.

title: Efficient Security Support for CXL Memory through Adaptive Incremental Offloaded (Re-)Encryption
problem: CXL memory expansion devices adopted in cloud TEE environments (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV) require XTS encryption for data confidentiality via CXL IDE, but XTS encryption's per-page latency causes significant performance overhead on memory-intensive workloads. Dynamically switching between CTR and XTS encryption modes and re-encrypting pages when access frequency changes incurs additional overhead that existing designs do not handle efficiently.
method: AIORE (Adaptive Incremental Offloaded Re-Encryption) combines CTR-mode encryption (low latency, parallelizable) for frequently accessed hot pages with XTS encryption (CXL IDE compliant) for cold pages. The framework dynamically selects the encryption scheme per page based on tracked access frequency using a lightweight monitoring mechanism. When a page's access pattern changes (cold-to-hot or hot-to-cold), AIORE performs incremental re-encryption, processing only the modified page rather than the entire memory region. Re-encryption is offloaded to computation resources within the CXL memory node itself, overlapping re-encryption with ongoing memory traffic to hide latency. The scheme is evaluated using gem5 full-system simulation across diverse benchmarks.
